templates.pattern: A water sample contains [M] mg of a pollutant dissolved in [V] litres of water. Calculate the pollutant concentration in mg/L.
templates.explanation:
Pollutant Concentration = Mass ÷ Volume
= [M] ÷ [V]
= [RESULT] mg/L

Concentration is the most fundamental measure in pollution science. mg/L is equivalent to parts per million (ppm) in water. Regulatory standards for drinking water and effluent discharge are typically expressed in these units.

templates.pattern: A pollutant has an original concentration of [C1] mg/L. After dilution it measures [C2] mg/L. Calculate the dilution factor.
templates.explanation:
Dilution Factor = Original Concentration ÷ Diluted Concentration
= [C1] ÷ [C2]
= [RESULT]

A dilution factor of [RESULT] means the solution was diluted [RESULT]-fold. Dilution is a key concept in understanding how pollutants spread and become less harmful in receiving water bodies.

templates.pattern: A wastewater sample uses [O] mg/L of dissolved oxygen over 5 days in a BOD test. Express the Biochemical Oxygen Demand per litre (mg/L).
templates.explanation:
BOD (Biochemical Oxygen Demand) = Oxygen consumed ÷ Volume
In a standard BOD₅ test the result is already expressed per litre.
BOD = [O] mg/L
= [RESULT] mg/L

BOD measures the amount of oxygen microorganisms need to break down organic matter. High BOD in rivers depletes dissolved oxygen, killing aquatic life. Clean river water has BOD < 2 mg/L; sewage can exceed 300 mg/L.

templates.pattern: The oxygen saturation level in a river at current temperature is [SAT] mg/L. The actual measured dissolved oxygen is [DO] mg/L. Calculate the dissolved oxygen deficit (mg/L).
templates.explanation:
DO Deficit = Saturation DO − Actual DO
= [SAT] − [DO]
= [RESULT] mg/L

DO deficit indicates how far a water body is from full oxygenation. A large deficit signals severe organic pollution. Fish generally need DO > 5 mg/L; values below 2 mg/L create hypoxic dead zones.

templates.pattern: A river carries a pollutant at a concentration of [C] mg/L with a flow rate of [Q] m³/s. Calculate the pollutant load in g/s.
templates.explanation:
Pollutant Load = Concentration × Flow Rate
= [C] mg/L × [Q] m³/s
= [C] mg/L × [Q] × 1000 L/m³ × (1 g / 1000 mg)
= [RESULT] g/s

Pollutant load (mass per unit time) is more informative than concentration alone because it accounts for how much water is carrying the pollutant. Two rivers with the same concentration but different flow rates deliver very different total pollutant masses.

templates.pattern: Acid rain has a hydrogen ion concentration of [H] × 10⁻⁵ mol/L. Calculate the pH. (Use pH = −log₁₀([H] × 10⁻⁵), round to 2 decimal places.)
templates.explanation:
pH = −log₁₀[H⁺]
= −log₁₀([H] × 10⁻⁵)
= [RESULT]

Normal rain has pH ≈ 5.6 due to dissolved CO₂. Acid rain caused by NOx and SO₂ emissions typically has pH 4–5. It damages aquatic ecosystems, leaches metals from soils, and corrodes buildings.

templates.pattern: A vehicle burns [F] litres of fuel and emits [E] g of NOx per litre of fuel burned. Calculate the total NOx emissions (g).
templates.explanation:
Total NOx Emission = Fuel Volume × Emission Factor
= [F] L × [E] g/L
= [RESULT] g

NOx (nitrogen oxides) are produced during high-temperature combustion when atmospheric nitrogen reacts with oxygen. They contribute to acid rain, ground-level ozone, and photochemical smog. Emission factors vary by engine type and fuel quality.

templates.pattern: An air quality monitor collects [MASS] µg of particulate matter on a filter over [VOL] m³ of sampled air. Calculate the PM2.5 concentration in µg/m³.
templates.explanation:
PM2.5 Concentration = Mass collected ÷ Volume of air sampled
= [MASS] µg ÷ [VOL] m³
= [RESULT] µg/m³

WHO guidelines recommend PM2.5 annual mean ≤ 5 µg/m³. PM2.5 particles penetrate deep into the lungs and bloodstream, causing respiratory and cardiovascular disease. Concentrations above 35 µg/m³ (24-hr mean) are considered unhealthy.

templates.pattern: A noise source measures [L1] dB at a distance of [D1] m. Using the inverse-square law, calculate the sound level (dB) at [D2] m. (Use: L2 = L1 − 20×log₁₀(D2/D1), round to 1 decimal place.)
templates.explanation:
Sound Level at distance: L2 = L1 − 20 × log₁₀(D2/D1)
= [L1] − 20 × log₁₀([D2]/[D1])
= [RESULT] dB

Every doubling of distance reduces sound level by approximately 6 dB. WHO recommends outdoor noise below 53 dB(A) during the day. Prolonged exposure above 85 dB causes permanent hearing damage.

templates.pattern: A radioactive contamination source has an activity of [A] Bq/m². The dose rate conversion factor is [CF] µSv/hr per Bq/m². Calculate the dose rate (µSv/hr).
templates.explanation:
Dose Rate = Activity × Conversion Factor
= [A] Bq/m² × [CF] µSv/hr per Bq/m² ÷ 1000
= [RESULT] µSv/hr

The becquerel (Bq) measures radioactive decay events per second. The sievert (Sv) measures biological radiation dose. Conversion factors depend on radionuclide type and energy. Background dose rate is typically 0.1–0.3 µSv/hr.
